<reason>CON built one structural thesis—a legally captive buyer cannot get market price discipline—and sharpened it every round: duopoly sellers, a prescriber-controlled exception valve, and outcomes contracts that only measure what the drugs reliably do. CON's pressure questions forced PRO into two answers (refunds for non-responders; exceptions unlock the non-preferred brand) that CON then converted into concessions in Rebuttal 2 and the closing. PRO's strongest live route—"the complications land on the same plan"—was met directly: the marginal mandated patient lacks the complication, discontinuation means the complication bill arrives anyway on top of a year of drug spend, and North Carolina's total spending rose rather than shifted. PRO never engaged the two-manufacturer point and answered the "priced into responders" objection with an assertion ("kills every pharmacy contract") that CON distinguished by noting other contracts rest on a buyer who can drop the drug entirely. PRO's closing line was memorable, but CON made the decisive comparison clearer. CON's two clipped turns are a real but small execution cost given the clips fell on final clauses.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A1/A2 in Rebuttal 2: it conceded that some indicated patients will be denied (owning the framing rather than dodging), then used PRO's own answers—non-responder refunds and documented exceptions unlocking the brand—to show sellers price refunds into responders and that formulary steering dissolves under "clinically indicated," collapsing PRO's price-discipline lever.</best_rebuttal>
